readingInstruction: Read Romans 15:14-16:27. Paul explains his ministry and plans, then sends a long list of greetings. Notice the names, especially the women and the many co-workers, and the closing doxology.
settingTheScene: Paul closes his letter by looking ahead. He has preached the gospel from Jerusalem to Illyricum, and now he plans to go to Spain, stopping in Rome on the way. First he must take the collection to Jerusalem. Chapter 16 reads like a list of names, but it is a window into the early church: women and men, slaves and free, Jews and Gentiles, house churches all over Rome. Every name stands for a real life changed by the gospel.
observation: “To be a minister of Christ Jesus to the Gentiles in the priestly service of the gospel of God” (15:16).
“And thus I make it my ambition to preach the gospel, not where Christ has already been named” (15:20).
“I hope to see you in passing as I go to Spain” (15:24).
“I commend to you our sister Phoebe, a servant of the church at Cenchreae” (16:1).
“Greet Prisca and Aquila, my fellow workers in Christ Jesus” (16:3).
“I appeal to you, brothers, to watch out for those who cause divisions and create obstacles contrary to the doctrine that you have been taught” (16:17).
“The God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet” (16:20).
“To the only wise God be glory forevermore through Jesus Christ! Amen” (16:27).
interpretation:
Paul begins with a compliment. He is satisfied that the Romans are full of goodness, filled with all knowledge, and able to instruct one another. Yet he has written boldly, as a reminder. He describes his ministry in priestly terms: he is “a minister of Christ Jesus to the Gentiles in the priestly service of the gospel of God, so that the offering of the Gentiles may be acceptable, sanctified by the Holy Spirit.” The Gentiles, brought to faith, are his offering to God.

His ambition is to preach where Christ has not been named. Now that this work in the eastern Mediterranean is complete, he looks west to Spain. He asks the Romans to help him on his journey. Before he goes, he must take the collection from Macedonia and Achaia to the poor saints in Jerusalem, a sign of unity between Gentile and Jewish believers. “I appeal to you, brothers… to strive together with me in your prayers to God on my behalf, that I may be delivered from the unbelievers in Judea.” Paul would indeed be arrested in Jerusalem, as we read in Acts, and reach Rome as a prisoner.

Chapter 16 begins with Phoebe, a servant (or deacon) of the church at Cenchreae, who very likely carried the letter to Rome. Paul calls her a “patron of many.” Next are Prisca and Aquila, who risked their necks for Paul and host a church in their house. Epaenetus, Mary, Andronicus and Junia, Ampliatus, Urbanus, Stachys, Apelles, and many others follow. Paul names about thirty people, with warm words: “beloved,” “fellow worker,” “approved in Christ,” “workers in the Lord.” Women feature prominently. The letter reminds us that the gospel is carried by ordinary people with extraordinary faithfulness. Christians differ about roles of women in church leadership, but all should honor the labor of these women.

Right in the middle comes a warning: “I appeal to you, brothers, to watch out for those who cause divisions and create obstacles contrary to the doctrine that you have been taught; avoid them. For such persons do not serve our Lord Christ, but their own appetites.” Doctrine matters, and unity is not unity at any price. But the promise comes: “The God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet.” This echoes Genesis 3:15.

Tertius, who wrote down the letter, adds his own greeting: “I Tertius, who wrote this letter, greet you in the Lord.” It is a delightful reminder that this great letter was dictated and written by a human scribe.

Then the final doxology. “Now to him who is able to strengthen you according to my gospel and the preaching of Jesus Christ, according to the revelation of the mystery that was kept secret for long ages but has now been disclosed and through the prophetic writings has been made known to all nations, according to the command of the eternal God, to bring about the obedience of faith, to the only wise God be glory forevermore through Jesus Christ! Amen.” The letter ends where it began: with the gospel, the Scriptures, the obedience of faith, and all nations. The mystery of the ages is revealed in Christ.
connection: Acts 18:1-3, 18-26 tell of Prisca and Aquila. Acts 20:1-3 shows Paul at Corinth when he wrote. Acts 21 to 28 tell what happened after the collection. 2 Corinthians 8 to 9 describe the collection. Genesis 3:15 promises the crushing of the serpent. Colossians 1:25-27 and Ephesians 3:1-13 speak of the mystery now revealed. 1 Corinthians 15:58 says our labor is not in vain. Philippians 2:25-30 speaks of Epaphroditus. 3 John and Titus 3:9-11 also warn about division.
application:
Write down the names of five people who have served you in the faith. Thank at least one of them this week.

Ask what your ambition is. Is there a place where Christ has not been named that God is calling you to?

Pray the last doxology as your own.
prayerPrompts: Thank God for those who have carried the gospel to you.
Ask him to make you a faithful servant of his church.
Praise him as the only wise God.
